author: mentor (Claude, 27 Oct 2026; v2 the same evening; v3 and v4 on 28 Oct: tips checked on the ~480-share research universe), for the organisation's agents to read at decision time; never training data
note: Each lesson says when it applies and how it is checked. 'test' names a check that mentor.py runs on our own daily data, so the lesson carries current numbers; lessons without one are experience, labelled as unverified until a test exists. Agents may use lessons as background, never as evidence to cite.

lessons.title: Four of our eight shares are banks
lessons.lesson: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank and SBI move together: an RBI surprise, a credit scare or foreign selling hits all four at once. Three banks in a top-3 portfolio is closer to one bet than three.

lessons.title: ITC and NTPC usually fall less than the banks
lessons.lesson: ITC (consumer staples) and NTPC (a regulated utility) tend to move less than the market; in a sell-off they often hold up better, and in a strong rally they often lag. Their low beta is a risk trait, not a forecast.

lessons.title: Momentum can fail sharply when a fall turns into a rebound
lessons.lesson: After a crash, the shares that fell most often rebound most, so a momentum rule holding the past winners can lag badly in the rebound months. Be cautious about momentum entries right after a deep market fall.

lessons.title: Trading costs decide small edges
lessons.lesson: Each rebalance pays brokerage, STT, charges and slippage (about 0.15% one way in our model). A strategy that trades monthly needs a real edge of several tenths of a percent a month just to stand still against holding the basket.

lessons.title: Results days carry gap risk
lessons.lesson: A share can jump or fall several percent on its quarterly results, regardless of its trend. A position opened a few days before results carries that event risk in addition to the signal; check the events calendar.

lessons.title: RBI and Fed decision days move rate-sensitive shares
lessons.lesson: Banks react most to RBI policy surprises, and the rupee and foreign flows react to the US Federal Reserve. A move just before a policy decision is often positioning, not a new trend.

lessons.title: Infosys earns in dollars
lessons.lesson: Most of Infosys' revenue is in foreign currency: a weaker rupee tends to help its margins, and US technology spending and US interest rates matter more to it than Indian demand.

lessons.title: Reliance is oil, retail and telecom at once
lessons.lesson: Reliance's earnings mix refining and petrochemicals (oil prices and margins), retail and Jio (telecom); news about one business, such as a listing of a unit, can move the share even when the others are unchanged.

lessons.title: An ex-dividend drop is not a loss
lessons.lesson: On the ex-date the price falls by about the dividend, which the holder receives; our scoring restates dividends, so judge the total return, never the price drop alone.

lessons.title: After SEVERE distribution days, falls are deeper
lessons.lesson: On our history, the 20 sessions after a SEVERE regime saw deeper average worst falls than after NORMAL days. It warns about risk; it did not time profitable exits, so size cautiously rather than sell everything.

lessons.title: The best backtest of the past rarely stays best
lessons.lesson: Choosing each year the idea with the best record over the previous years lost to the basket on our history. Trust live, pre-registered results over any backtest, including your own reasoning about why something worked.

lessons.title: Small positions pay a fixed charge on every sale
lessons.lesson: Every sale pays a fixed depository charge of about Rs 16, whatever its size. On a small position that dwarfs the percentage costs, so selling and re-buying a share to adjust a weight a little is rarely worth it at our size; prefer fewer, larger, slower changes.

lessons.title: Big moves come in clusters
lessons.lesson: A violent day is usually followed by more violent days, and calm by calm. After a large move, expect more large moves in either direction: it is a reason to size down, not a forecast of direction.

lessons.title: Below the 200-day average, falls run deeper
lessons.lesson: When the market sits below its long-term average, the next weeks' worst falls tend to be deeper. It says to be careful with new buys and their size; on our history it did not reliably say when to sell.

lessons.title: Several shares are safer than one, but only if they differ
lessons.lesson: Holding several shares cuts the swings of a portfolio, because they do not all fall together; shares from the same sector (our four banks) cut it much less. Check what else you already hold before adding a share that behaves like it.

lessons.title: A loss needs a bigger gain to recover
lessons.lesson: A 20% fall needs a 25% gain to get back, a 33% fall needs 50%, and a 50% fall needs 100%. Avoiding a deep loss matters more than catching every gain, which is why exits are always allowed and new buys can pause.

lessons.title: Start from the base rate, then adjust
lessons.lesson: Before arguing a case, ask how often this kind of call works in general. A share rises by more than costs in only about half of months, so a confident call needs evidence that this time differs, and a call without it is a coin flip with costs.

lessons.title: Patience is taxed less
lessons.lesson: In India a gain on shares held over 12 months is taxed at the long-term rate (12.5%), a shorter holding at the short-term rate (20%). A strategy that sells within the year gives up part of every gain; holding longer keeps more of it compounding.

lessons.title: Results come in seasons
lessons.lesson: Indian companies report quarterly results mostly in the weeks after each quarter ends (mid-January, April, July and October). Across the market those weeks are only slightly more stock-specific (about 2% more spread); the real risk is each company's own results day, so check the calendar before a call on a share about to report.

lessons.title: Most news is already in the price
lessons.lesson: By the time a headline reaches us, professional traders have usually acted on it. Ask what the news changes that the market has not yet priced, such as a lasting change in earnings, and treat a story everyone is reading as weak evidence for a trade.

lessons.title: Size a position by what you can lose on it
lessons.lesson: Decide first how much of the budget a wrong call may cost, then size the position so that a realistic bad move costs no more. A high-conviction idea still gets a bounded size: conviction is often highest just before being wrong.

lessons.title: A big one-day move says little about the next week
lessons.lesson: Chasing a share that just jumped 5% is not an edge: on average the next week roughly matched the market. A big drop is not a bargain by itself either: it tended to lag a little more. Ask what changed, not how far it moved.

lessons.title: Buying near a 52-week low showed no edge
lessons.lesson: A share sitting near its 52-week low did no better than the market over the next month (slightly worse, not clearly). Cheapness after a fall is not a reason to buy by itself; wait for a reason the fall has ended.

lessons.title: Much of the gain came around the turn of the month
lessons.lesson: The last session of a month and the first three of the next carried about half of the average share's gains. Avoid needless selling into the turn of the month; a monthly rebalance's timing matters.

lessons.title: A fixed 10% stop cuts the worst losses but costs return
lessons.lesson: A stop caps the damage of the worst holdings, but it also sells many shares that recover, and lowers the average return; with overnight gaps a real stop fills worse than tested. Use a stop to limit risk, not as a source of profit.
